  "text": "The bottom drawer in the kitchen had stuck every winter since Owen moved in. His mother opened it by pressing her knee against the cupboard and pulling with both hands.

“There’s a knack,” she said.

Inside were tea towels, birthday candles, and instructions for appliances they no longer owned.

Owen was home for three days. His room had become a place for drying clothes, though she had cleared the bed before he arrived.

On Saturday morning, he found her kneeling beside the drawer.

“Looking for something?”

“The good scissors.”

He pulled. The handle came away in his hand.

Neither of them spoke.

“I’ll get a new one,” he said.

“They won’t have the same.”

At the hardware shop, he bought two plain handles and a sheet of sandpaper. Back in the kitchen, he emptied the drawer onto the table.

His mother picked through the papers while he worked on the swollen edges.

“Your father kept everything.”

“So do you.”

She folded a yellowed receipt and put it in the bin.

The drawer slid in crookedly. Owen took it out and tried again.

“Tea?” she asked.

“In a minute.”

When he finished, both drawers had matching handles. His mother opened the bottom one, then closed it with a finger.

On Sunday, she stood by the door while he checked his pockets.

“You’ve left your charger.”

He went back for it. In the kitchen, the spare screws were in a jam jar, and the instructions for the new kettle lay flat on the table.

“Shall I put these away?” he called.

“Bottom drawer,” she said. “There’s room now.”"
